name: Panjal Athirathram (Athirathram Yajna)
tagline: A 12‑day Agnicayana — Panjal’s ancient Vedic fire‑altar ritual
summary: Athirathram at Panjal is a rare 12‑day Śrauta Agnicayana (fire‑altar) yajna, noted for its bird‑shaped altar built from 1005 bricks and performed in Panjal in 1975 and again in 2011.
description: Athirathram (Agnicayana) is one of the most elaborate Śrauta yajnas in the Vedic tradition: a multi‑day Soma and fire ritual that reconstructs the cosmic order by building a bird‑shaped northern altar (uttaravedi) from precisely measured bricks and reciting long śruti texts.

Panjal, a small village in Thrissur district, is famed as a yajna‑site (yajna bhūmi) because major Athirathrams were held there in 1975 and revived in 2011. The 1975 performance was recorded by scholars and later featured in studies of the ritual; the 2011 event drew national and international attention and visiting researchers.

For visitors the attraction is cultural and acoustic: sustained Vedic chanting, ritual construction of the altar, scholarly seminars and a sense of continuity with a living oral tradition. Panjal also retains local temples and Mana (traditional Namboothiri households) connected with the sajjana (ritual organizers).

This is a sacred and highly structured rite preserved by trained Vedic practitioners; visitors should treat the yagashala (ritual ground) as a consecrated space and confirm programme details with organisers before travelling.
highlights: A 12‑day Athirathram / Agnicayana ritual with night offerings (athirātram = ‘beyond night’).
Construction of a bird‑shaped uttaravedi from precisely counted bricks (traditional accounts cite 1005 bricks).
Major performances at Panjal recorded in 1975 and revived in 2011, drawing scholars and international observers.
Documented in academic studies and widely reported by Indian press during the 2011 revival.
Linked to nearby Lakshmi Narayana temple and traditional Namboothiri manas (houses) in Panjal.

sections.heading: Background
body: Athirathram (Agnicayana) belongs to the classical Śrauta corpus: ritual procedures anchored in the Yajurveda and other Vedic śuktas. The rite symbolically rebuilds the cosmos by constructing an altar with carefully measured layers of bricks and performing Soma offerings across many sessions.

Panjal acquired recognition as a recurring venue for large yagas; a notable Athirathram there was performed in 1975 and again in April 2011, when organisers and academic observers reopened the ancient practice for study and public witnessing.

sections.heading: Ritual practice — what happens
body: The full Athirathram runs across several days (traditionally twelve) and includes multiple Soma offerings, continuous chanting and the step‑by‑step erection of the uttaravedi. Technical features include geometric layout, exact brick counts and alignment with cardinal directions — a reason scholars study the rite for its mathematical and astronomical knowledge.

Visually the ritual centres on the yagashala (temporary ritual ground), the homa kundas (fire pits) and the bird‑shaped altar. During the 2011 event organisers also arranged seminars, exhibitions and documentation for researchers; earlier accounts record processions of bricks and community participation in preparatory rites.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Panjal is a village near Chelakkara and was reported in contemporary coverage as being close to Shoranur railway station (local distance references appear in press coverage of the 2011 event). There is no fixed schedule for Athirathram — performances are rare and organised by specialist Vedic trusts and communities — so confirm dates, visitor rules and entry with organisers before travelling.

When attending: wear modest clothing, respect restricted zones around the yagashala, ask permission before photographing ritual priests, and expect long periods of chanting and formal procedures. Check local temple timetables and panchayat contacts for logistics; the ritual site and arrangements change with each performance.

visitorInfo.bestTime: No fixed season — Athirathram is staged rarely; past Panjal performances occurred in April (1975, 2011); check organisers for exact dates.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Panjal lies in Thrissur district (near Chelakkara / Shoranur). Use Shoranur or Thrissur as railheads and travel by road to the village; confirm local directions and yagashala location with organisers before you go.
etiquette: Athirathram is a consecrated ritual — observe silence and decorum near the yagashala.
Ask organisers about public viewing areas and photography rules; parts of the ritual may be restricted.
Confirm dates and visitor permissions well in advance — these yagas are scheduled rarely and require local coordination.
If you are researching the ritual, request access to organisers or scholars; recent performances have included academic documentation.
